# AGENTS.md

Rules for AI coding agents working in this repo. Humans follow them too.

- Hackathon repo (EHL Grand Finale, Munich, 10 to 11 Oct 2026). Code freeze and Live Final
  Sunday 12:00. Working agent first, polish second.
- Do not preserve backward compatibility. Remove obsolete paths instead of adding
  compatibility layers, fallbacks, or migrations.
- Choose the simplest implementation that fully meets the current requirement.
  No speculative abstractions, configuration, or indirection.
- Grow the system in layers: smallest version that works end to end, then add on
  top of a product that already works. Never trade a working product for
  unfinished complexity.
- Keep components modular and concerns separated.
- Prefer established libraries already in the project before adding new ones or
  writing your own implementation. Read `arena_kit` (in `.venv`) before writing a helper:
  the cost function, quote parsing, data lookup and the runners already exist.
- Never commit secrets. Keys go into `.env` (gitignored). Never print, log or paste the
  arena key anywhere (code, logs, issues, Discord, PR text).
- All changes go through a pull request against `main`, reviewed by one teammate.
  Branch naming: `<firstname>/<topic>`.
- No em-dashes in prose or user-facing copy.
- Be terse: after an action, state what changed in three lines or fewer.

## Challenge: Tacto Negotiation Arena

We are the purchasing team of Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional German pump maker. Our agent
negotiates by e-mail with Tacto's supplier bots (LLM personas with hidden economics) and closes
one term sheet per case, or walks away. Full text: `docs/challenge.md` (brief), `docs/api.md`
(API, claim checks, cost formula), `docs/submission.md`. Upstream:
https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit, FAQ: https://arena.tacto.ai/faq.

**Score.** Per case `(C_open - C_deal) / (C_open - C_best)`, clipped to 0..1. C is the total
cost in euros over the case horizon: price, uncovered need, payment terms, freight, lead time,
quality, tooling, index clause, and in `stabilise` / `secure_supply` cases a charge for leaving
the supplier below a sustainable margin. Not price. `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C exactly.
No deal scores the alternative (0 if none). A broken must-have scores 0.

**Live Final.** Sunday 12:00, five waves of hidden cases, 8 minutes each, all cases of a wave in
parallel. New suppliers; up to a third combine supplier and case types practice never shows.
Some cite the Sunday 08:00 data release. Wave score = mean case score x 100; total = sum.

**Hard rules (breaking one can disqualify us):**
- No human in the loop during the final. The runner is started before 12:00 and left alone.
- Agent code never calls `/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`,
  `/leaderboard`, `/v1/leaderboard`, `/results`, `/v1/results`. Those are for people.
- One key per team. No attacks on the arena or other teams.
- The final runs the commit we submit at 12:00. No pushes after that.

**Hard limits:**
- 60 seconds per message per thread, counted from the supplier's reply. A late message is a
  timeout; three in a row end the thread. Heavy work happens before a session is opened.
- 10 messages per thread (case `round_limit`), up to 3 term sheets per message, every term sheet
  carries every `negotiable` field.
- Max 3 claim checks per message; one argument per sentence, ID and figure in the same sentence.
  An unknown ID or wrong figure is `contradicted` and costs trust.
- 10 calls per second and 10 open sessions per key.
- **Practice quota: 200 sessions per rolling 24 h for the whole team, shared across all
  machines.** Sandbox (`case:D01`, `case:D02`) and the local simulator are free.

## Repo map

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `buyer/agent.py` | the case coordinator: the brief per supplier (persona, floor, anchor, target, levers, claims), the blackboard, the decision to close |
| `buyer/thread.py` | one move in one supplier thread: read the reply, policy, e-mail, guard |
| `buyer/economics.py` | every number: C of a package, floor, anchor, probe sheets, concessions, the accept gate |
| `buyer/claims.py` | the claim bank: pre-verified data sentences, figure next to ID, as the arena checks them |
| `buyer/personas.py` | supplier archetype, levers, tone and relationship guard from the data; refined from the first reply |
| `buyer/llm.py` | the model: reads a reply into signals, words the e-mail; hard timeouts, None on failure |
| `buyer/guard.py` | last check on an outgoing body: no leaks, no unknown IDs, no foreign figures; the template e-mail |
| `buyer/runner.py` | one negotiator per thread in parallel; practice and Live Final runners |
| `buyer/cli.py` | `buyer play`, `buyer run`, `buyer plan`, `buyer pull` |
| `logs/*.jsonl` | plans, moves and cases as JSON lines, gitignored |
| `tests/` | end to end against `arena-sim`, no network, no model |
| `docs/` | brief, API, submission guide (copied from upstream) |
| `data/package/` | the data package, gitignored; `uv run arena data` fetches it (Sunday also `data/release-sunday/`) |
| `logs/sessions/<set>/` | finished sessions with trace and back office, gitignored; `uv run buyer pull` fetches them |

`arena_kit` (Tacto's starter kit) is a git dependency pinned in `pyproject.toml`. We do not patch
it; we wrap it. Its README is the best guide to its modules:
https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit/tree/main/starter-kit

## Commands

```sh
uv sync                                         # install (Python 3.12)
uv run arena data                               # data package into data/ (again Sunday after 08:00)
uv run arena me                                 # key works? quota left?
uv run pytest -q && uv run ruff check .         # before every PR
uv run buyer plan case:P01                      # the case brief, no session, no quota
uv run buyer play case:D01 -v                   # sandbox: free, real supplier bots
uv run buyer play case:P01 -v                   # practice: costs 1 of the team's 200
uv run buyer run --set practice --parallel 10   # all 10 hosted practice cases: costs 10
uv run buyer pull --set practice                # every finished session -> logs/sessions/
uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10      # the Live Final, Sunday before 12:00
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package   # local API with a scripted supplier
```

`--agent naive` plays the kit's baseline instead of ours. The MCP server `arena-data`
(`.mcp.json`) gives coding agents SQL, ID lookup and documents over the data package.

## Working on the negotiation agent

- **Code owns numbers, the model owns words.** Every binding value (term sheets, accept,
  walk away) is computed or checked in code with `total_cost` and `must_haves_ok`. Every figure
  in an e-mail comes from code, next to its data ID. The model reads the supplier and writes.
- **The floor is always a real number.** Full cost per unit from the supplier's cost breakdown
  (when it sends one), else the should-cost fact, else the quote less the margin the stance
  estimates in it; plus the margin we leave. A breakdown arriving mid-case lowers floor and target.
- **The model proposes the stance, code clamps it.** Opening gap, capture, margin, justified share
  and concession steps are set per supplier from the dossier at case open, inside ranges by tier
  and goal (`economics.STANCE_RANGES`); the constants are the fallback, never the answer. Every
  stance is logged with its reason so practice can judge it.
- **Never accept** a term sheet that breaks a must-have or costs more than the alternative.
  Price unstated fields at the supplier's standard terms from its quote PDF (`docs.standard_terms`).
- **Generalise, don't memorise.** No logic keyed on practice case IDs or supplier IDs. Knowledge
  derived from the data package at runtime is fine; it must also work for unseen suppliers.
- **Read the supplier.** What moves it is in the data: call notes, letters, news, quote
  remarks, payment history, scorecards. Trade what is cheap for us (payment days, contract
  length, volume, dates) for what it values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, budget, a missing alternative or the target price.
- **Every model call has a hard timeout** well under 60 s, and the move still goes out if it
  fails. Measure latency per move.

## The learning loop

1. Try on the simulator or the sandbox first. Spend practice quota only on a change you expect
   to help, and check `uv run arena me` before batch runs: teammates share the 200.
2. After practice: `uv run buyer pull`, then read `logs/sessions/`. The trace holds the supplier's
   reasons for every move, the back office its internal discussion, the result the cost breakdown.
3. Find why C_deal missed C_best (which lever, which argument, which timing), change the agent,
   score candidate term sheets offline with `total_cost`, then play again.
4. Write what you learned about supplier behaviour into the PR description, so the team and
   the pitch can use it.

## Sunday

- 08:00: `uv run arena data` again; the release lands in `data/release-sunday/`.
- 09:00: pre-flight, one practice case through the final machine and setup.
- 11:30: checklist in `docs/submission.md` (key, data, LLM credits, power, no sleep, log file).
- Before 12:00: start `uv run buyer run --set final --parallel 10 -v 2>&1 | tee logs/final.log`
  from `main`, submit that commit hash on ehl.gg.
- [Tacto Negotiation Arena project](tacto-negotiation-arena-project.md) — challenge, repo layout, policy doc location, weekend timeline

## Working on the negotiation agent

- **Code owns numbers, the model owns words.** Every binding value (term sheets, accept,
  walk away) is computed or checked in code with `total_cost` and `must_haves_ok`. Every figure
  in an e-mail comes from code, next to its data ID. The model reads the supplier and writes.
- **The floor is always a real number.** Full cost per unit from the supplier's cost breakdown
  (when it sends one), else the should-cost fact, else the quote less the margin the stance
  estimates in it; plus the margin we leave. A breakdown arriving mid-case lowers floor and target.
- **The model proposes the stance, code clamps it.** Opening gap, capture, margin, justified share
  and concession steps are set per supplier from the dossier at case open, inside ranges by tier
  and goal (`economics.STANCE_RANGES`); the constants are the fallback, never the answer. Every
  stance is logged with its reason so practice can judge it.

  Price unstated fields at the supplier's standard terms from its quote PDF (`docs.standard_terms`).

  derived from the data package at runtime is fine; it must also work for unseen suppliers.

  remarks, payment history, scorecards. Trade what is cheap for us (payment days, contract
  length, volume, dates) for what it values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, budget, a missing alternative or the target price.
- **Every model call has a hard timeout** well under 60 s, and the move still goes out if it
  fails. Measure latency per move.

coordinator: code prepares the case from data, checks every supplier fact, and sets every

The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:

- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.

- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

# Buyer Agent: How the System Works

10 Oct 2026, Julian

Our agent negotiates each case as a team of parallel thread negotiators under one case
coordinator: code prepares the case from data, checks every supplier fact, and sets every term;
the LLM only reads replies and writes e-mails.

## Architecture

Personas and claims are built once before the final. During a wave, every supplier thread loops
reader → fact check → policy → writer → guard; only the code steps set numbers.

(System architecture diagram: offline preparation, live wave, thread negotiator loop. See the
source PDF.)

## A case, step by step

1. **Wave starts.** The wave runner sees the new cases and starts one case coordinator per case,
   up to 10 in parallel.
2. **Prepare (within 20 s).** The coordinator opens the session and builds a case brief from data:
   costs (C_open, our alternative, target, walk-away), the lever table, a view of each supplier,
   market facts and a claim bank of verified arguments. Unknown suppliers or parts go through the
   fallback cascade. A stance call proposes each supplier's negotiation parameters, clamped by
   code.
3. **Negotiate in parallel.** One thread negotiator per supplier runs a loop each round:
   1. The reader turns the supplier's e-mail into signals and factual statements.
   2. The fact checker tests each statement against our data.
   3. The policy engine picks the next term sheets and claims, or decides to accept or walk.
   4. The writer turns that decision into an e-mail.
   5. The guard checks it and sends it.
4. **Close.** The coordinator accepts the best sheet that keeps every must-have and beats our
   alternative, or walks away. It closes at the latest 90 s before the wave's cap.
5. **Learn.** The full trace and what we learned about each supplier are stored for the next
   practice run.

## The modules

| Module | Job | In → out | Run by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wave runner (`runner.py`) | Polls the final's case list, starts a coordinator per case, restarts after a crash | Case list → running cases | Code |
| Case coordinator (`agent.py`) | Builds the case brief, starts thread negotiators, keeps the shared blackboard, decides when to close | Case file + personas + data → brief, final accept or walk | Code |
| Fallback cascade | Fills gaps for unknown suppliers or parts: case facts, database search, category averages, the supplier's own documents, web context last | Unknown ID → filled fields with source and confidence | Code; web search time-boxed |
| Personas (`personas.py`, `knowledge/`) | One profile per supplier: archetype with evidence, levers, tone, history | Data + past negotiations → persona JSON | LLM offline, code live |
| Claim bank (`claims.py`) | Arguments as sentences with figure and data ID, computed exactly as the arena checks them | Data → verified claims, ranked per supplier | Code |
| Economics (`economics.py`) | Total cost C of any sheet, floor, anchor, target, probe sheets, concession steps, accept gate | Case + brief + stance + signals → term sheets and limits | Code |
| Reader (`llm.py`) | Reads a supplier e-mail: signals (approval needed, walk risk, mood, cheaper variant) and factual statements | E-mail → JSON | Small LLM, hard timeout |
| Fact checker | Tests each supplier statement against the data: confirmed, contradicted, selective or unverifiable (not built yet) | Statements → verdicts and rebuttal claims | Code |
| Policy engine | Chooses the next move from goal, case type, archetype, verdicts and time left | Brief + thread state → sheets, claims, tone, or accept/walk | Code |
| Writer (`llm.py`) | Turns the chosen move into a short business e-mail | Move → e-mail text | Small LLM; template if late |
| Guard (`guard.py`) | Blocks leaks, unknown IDs, figures the plan did not set, broken must-haves; adds missing claims | Draft → safe message | Code |
| Knowledge and logs | Append-only negotiation log, full traces, per-move log, findings | Every move and trace → files in git | Code |

## Most important data

Nine data sources feed the case brief, ranked by impact on the score: the case file and the quote
decide C directly; the rest decide how far a supplier will move and why.

| # | Data | What it decides |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Case file and quote PDF: need, horizon, rates, must-haves, alternative, term options, standard terms | C directly, including the uncovered-need trap |
| 2 | Supplier cost floor: should-cost, cost drivers, cost-breakdown spreadsheet | Anchor, target and the margin penalty |
| 3 | Index values for the supplier's cost drivers | The justified price change, our strongest verified claims, the basis of the fact check |
| 4 | Letters, notes and news per supplier | What actually moves it (cash, capacity, relationship), plus notice periods |
| 5 | Negotiation history: asked vs. settled per supplier | The best prior for how far it moves |
| 6 | Supplier intel and our invoice history: credit index, equity, ownership, our late payments | The archetype and the payment lever |
| 7 | Contracts, clauses and sourcing | Notice periods, index clauses, expiry dates, single-sourcing |
| 8 | Scorecards and quality notifications | The quality lever |
| 9 | Forecasts, past order prices, rival quotes | Volume growth, price history and rivals as arguments |

## Stance and fallback constants

Since draft two, the opening gap, capture, margin, justified share, concession steps and the margin
estimated in the quote form a stance that the model proposes per supplier at case open, from the
dossier (profile, signals, letter, quote, cost data, rivals). Code clamps each value to a range by
tier and goal and logs it with a one-sentence reason. The constants below are the fallback when the
stance call times out.

Tiers come from the persona: strategic covers castings, seals and electrical parts, A suppliers and
single sources; important and standard follow the persona's tier.

How a stance becomes a live value (clamps in code, every value logged with its reason):

1. **Stance:** the model's proposal for this supplier, or the fallback constant for its tier and
   goal.
2. **Clamps and data checks:** each value stays inside its tier and goal range. The anchor never
   goes below the floor, built from full cost in order of trust: the supplier's cost-breakdown
   XLSX, else should-cost, else the quote less the stance's margin estimate. Price increases start
   from the weighted justified increase.
3. **Live signals, within fixed bounds:** `needs_approval` multiplies steps by 0.7;
   `walk_risk: high` stops price pushes; a cool mood warms the next e-mail but keeps the terms.

| Fallback constant | Values | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GOAL_CAPTURE` | leverage 0.75, routine 0.5, stabilise 0.6, secure_supply 0.55, quality_first 0.65 | Share of the possible saving (opening quote's C down to our best estimate) to reach before accepting; higher means pushing longer | Leverage case: accept once 75 % of the possible saving is in hand |
| `OPENING_GAP` | strategic 0.05, important 0.08, standard 0.12 | How far below the supplier's quote the first offer anchors; never below the floor; not used in price-increase cases | Quote €100, standard supplier: first offer €88 |
| `TIER_MARGIN` | strategic 4 %, important 2 %, standard 0 % | Margin left above the supplier's estimated full cost when setting the floor. In `stabilise` / `secure_supply` the case's `sustainable_margin_pct` replaces it; standard suppliers are capped at 3 % | Full cost €90, strategic: floor €93.60 |
| `JUSTIFIED_SHARE` | strategic 0.5, important 0.25, standard 0.0 | In price-increase cases, share of the data-justified increase offered in round 1 | Justified +2.3 %: strategic first offer +1.2 %, standard +0 % |
| `STEPS` | 35 %, 25 %, 15 %, 10 % of the remaining gap; 60 % once the tier's price pushes are used | Size of each concession, made only after the supplier moved; the 60 % step closes fast when we may not push further | Gap €10: concede €3.50, then €1.63, then €0.73 |

Tuning rule: one constant per batch of 10 practice cases, each case replayed twice before a change
is credited, every result logged in `docs/findings.md`.

## Draft-two results (sandbox, 10 Oct)

On the free sandbox, draft two reached 0.96 on D01 and 0.54 on D02, with every claim verified after
run 1 and no timeouts. No practice quota was used. Latency was 11 to 19 s per move (reader plus
writer, `claude-opus-5-5` at low effort); the stance call adds 9 to 11 s once at case open.

Replays: D01, D02. The single contradicted claim (run 1) was a package ID cited in the demo world.

| Run | D01: price increase, strategic foundry | D02: RFQ, two job shops | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.73, deal €50.90, 2 rounds | 0.37, deal €15.30, 3 rounds | Draft-two port, constants from the plan |
| 2 | 0.93, deal €49.90, 4 rounds | 0.43, deal €15.00 | Own-world claims, supplier-friendly tie-breaks, floor below the opening gap, hold a round while the supplier moves |
| 3 | 0.84, agreed €50.37, 2 rounds | 0.32, deal €15.50 | First model-proposed stance (too cautious) |
| 4 | 0.84 (bound by the same floor) | 0.54, final offer €14.50, 5 rounds | Calibrated stance prompt, 3 % margin cap for standard suppliers, closer waits while the supplier moves |
| 5 | 0.96, agreed €49.65, 4 rounds | not run | Floor on the case's sustainable margin |

### What changed, and why

- **A real floor every time.** Before, a supplier without should-cost got a floor at 90 % of its
  quote, which clipped the opening gap.
- **The margin we leave is the case's number.** The arena charges only below
  `sustainable_margin_pct`, and only in `stabilise` and `secure_supply`. Draft one's 8 % strategic
  rule bound the D01 anchor at 0.84; the case's 4 % gave 0.96.
- **The stance needed calibration.** Its first proposals were more cautious than the constants
  (7 % gap, margin on top of margin) and D02 fell to 0.32. A paragraph with the concessions seen so
  far plus the 3 % cap fixed it: 0.54.
- **Closing.** At the target, hold one more round while the supplier still moves and rounds
  remain; the stall rule no longer accepts a moving supplier. In run 1, D01 accepted after 2 rounds
  with 8 left.
- **Claims.** A case whose refs the package does not know cites only its own facts. Rival offers
  are cited only after the bidder's first reply and only when cheaper.
- **Sheets.** Among options that cost us the same, take the one the supplier prefers: 35 days'
  lead time instead of 21, which the job shop had priced with overtime.

### Next
